entries.title: Vikings lose wide receiver Justin Jefferson in 23-16 win over Buccaneers
entries.summary: <p>TAMPA, Fla. — Myles Price returned a punt 86 yards for a score, Kyler Murray threw a 41-yard TD pass to Jordan Addison and the Minnesota Vikings beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 23-16 on Sunday.</p><p>It was a costly game for both teams.</p><p>Baker Mayfield hurt his thumb on a desperation pass late in the fourth quarter. He was screaming in pain on the ground before walking off and was replaced by rookie Jalon Daniels in the final minute.</p><p>Two-time All-Pro wide receiver Justin Jefferson didn't return for Minnesota after injuring his right ankle in the first quarter.</p><p>The Vikings are 3-0 for the second time in three years. The Buccaneers are 0-3 for the first time since 2014, when they finished 2-14 and got the No. 1 overall draft pick, taking Jameis Winston.</p><p>Murray was 15 of 29 for 168 yards with one TD pass and one interception in his first full game with the Vikings. He sustained a concussion in the first quarter of the season opener and Carson Wentz led Minnesota to consecutive wins.</p><p>Mayfield hasn't played like a $55 million-a-year quarterback since the Buccaneers gave him a $165 million extension before the season. He was 17 of 34 for 217 yards with one TD and one interception, taking six sacks.</p><p>Tampa Bay's woeful offense couldn't do much against coordinator Brian Flores' defense.</p><p>Mayfield had an 85-yard touchdown pass to Chris Godwin Jr. on third-and-30 negated by a holding penalty on Luke Goedeke in the third quarter.</p><p>That summed up the offense's struggles.</p><p>Mayfield's 14-yard scramble on second-and-9 later was negated by a holding penalty on Payne Durham. But the Bucs got a first down on third-and-29 when Joshua Metellus hit Emeka Egbuka helmet-to-helmet. Again, the offense had to settle for a field goal. Chase McLauglin's 54-yarder cut it to 17-16.</p><p>Will Reichard's 56-yard field goal extended Minnesota's lead to 20-16 with 3:10 remaining. He added a 43-yarder to cap the scoring.</p><p>Murray connected with Addison on a deep throw on third-and-8 to give the Vikings a 17-10 lead in the second quarter. Addison beat Jacob Parrish in one-on-one coverage, making a smooth adjustment on the ball.</p><p>After A'Shawn Robinson intercepted Murray's pass to set up a first down at the Vikings 22 in the third quarter, the Bucs went nowhere. Bucky Irving ran 3 yards and then dropped a pass. Mayfield got sacked on third down and McLaughlin's 38-yarder cut it to 17-13.</p><p>The Buccaneers fell behind 10-0 after just one possession. Following a three-and-out, Price darted up the middle, cut to the right and sprinted down the sideline for his first career touchdown.</p><p>Mayfield fired a 40-yard TD pass down the seam to rookie Ted Hurst III to cut it to 10-7.</p><p>The Buccaneers had a first down at Minnesota's 7 after Mayfield and Cade Otton connected on a 37-yard pass. But consecutive holding penalties on Cody Mauch and Graham Barton derailed the drive and McLaughlin kicked a 28-yard field goal to tie it.</p><h3>Brotherly love</h3><p>Buccaneers left guard Ben Bredeson played against his younger brother, Vikings rookie fullback Max Bredeson. Their older brother, Jack, is the director of player information for the New York Mets. All three went to Michigan.</p><h3>Injuries</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Vikings:</b> Jefferson injured his right ankle when a defender fell on it. He walked to the locker room after watching a couple series. ... P Brett Thorson (hamstring) was inactive. ... CB Charles Demmings left with a hamstring injury.</p><p><b>Buccaneers:</b> Edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr. (groin) and LB Josiah Trotter (shoulder) were inactive. ... WR Jalen McMillan left in the first quarter with a knee injury and didn't return.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Vikings:</b> Host Miami next Sunday.</p><p><b>Buccaneers:</b> Host Green Bay next Sunday.<br></p>

entries.title: Lyons' EJ Kuhlman is on a roll
entries.summary: <p>Playing high school football and baseball keeps Lyons senior EJ Kuhlman pretty busy.</p><p>But what does he do in his downtime?</p><p>“I love playing pickleball with my friends,” Kuhlman told the Sun-Times. “I think that’s actually got me on my toes.”</p><p>There’s no doubt the 5-9, 177-pound Kuhlman’s footwork is elite.</p><p>He’s in his second season as the lead running back for the Lions (5-1, 2-1 West Suburban Silver), who have clinched their sixth consecutive IHSA playoff berth.</p><p>Last year against York in the regular season, Kuhlman ran 43 times for a program-record 246 yards. Some other records could be in play this season, but he’s not interested in talking about them.</p><p>“My main goal is just winning conference first,” he said. “I don’t really care about the stuff that comes with it.</p><p>“I mean, it’s awesome to get those records at the end of the season, see what you’ve achieved. But you can’t really put all that credit on yourself . . . because you know a lot of that comes from coaches and O-linemen.”</p><p>He had 1,104 rushing yards and 15 touchdowns last fall and has scored at least one touchdown in every game this season with multiple 100-yard rushing games.</p><p>It’s a culmination of everything Kuhlman has been working toward.</p><p>“I always played flag football growing up, but I didn’t start tackle until seventh grade,” he said. “I was with the LFC [Lyons Football Club] program, and it was with a lot of my same buddies I play with now.”</p><p>Like most kids, Kuhlman tried a variety of sports growing up: soccer, basketball, tennis and wrestling in addition to the ones he’s still doing.</p><p>“You kind of play whatever your parents put you in,” he said. “Sports has always been part of my life, and it’s a big part of me and who I am.”</p><p>Until last year, Kuhlman didn’t really favor one sport over the other.</p><p>“Honestly, I was always split between baseball and football,” he said. “But junior year, I think I took football a lot more serious. I think I started to appreciate it a lot more. The amount of effort that goes into football is kind of what took me to love football more than baseball.</p><p>“But I still love both sports, very close to equal. But football is just a little different for me.”</p><p>That meant an extra level of preparation for his final high school season, focusing primarily on getting faster.</p><p>“Speed’s the biggest factor with a running back,” he said. “So you drop a couple of pounds to gain that extra point-one or point-two on that 40 [yard dash time].</p><p>“But I think this year, my goal is just to try not to get down — always break that first guy.”</p><p>The season of experience has paid off in other ways.</p><p>“What [is] different this year is kind of [being] comfortable,” Kuhlman said. “And I feel like [it’s been] to slow the game down and just realize that you kind of control it.”</p>

entries.title: Man charged with shooting of 1-year-old girl in Chicago Lawn home
entries.summary: <p>A man was charged with the shooting Saturday of a 1-year-old girl in a Chicago Lawn home on the South Side. </p><p>Davaris Washington, 38, was charged with reckless discharge of a firearm, unlawful use of a machine gun, reckless conduct causing great bodily harm and possession of a firearm by a repeat offender, Chicago police said. </p><p>Washington was arrested around 12:15 a.m. Saturday in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/26/girl-found-shot-inside-chicago-lawn-home" target="_blank" >6400 block of South Mozart Street</a> where the girl was found shot minutes earlier, police said. </p><p>She was taken to Comer Children's Hospital in critical condition, officials said. </p><p>Washington is expected to appear in court Monday. </p>

entries.title: Cubs! White Sox! Playoffs! Keep chanting those words and maybe, just maybe, it'll last more than a few days
entries.summary: <p>Are you ready for both the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> in the playoffs?</p><p>For God’s sake, somebody has to be.</p><p>Are the Cubs themselves ready? It’s a bit hard to believe in that after they spent the final days of the regular season losing back-to-back critical games at Wrigley Field to the going-nowhere Marlins, then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-doubleheader-tampa-playoff-rotation-mlb-postseason-clay-holmes-david-peterson" target="_blank" >gagging on both ends of a doubleheader</a> in Boston, to rob themselves of a sweet chance at home-field advantage in a wild-card series against the Padres that starts Tuesday.</p><p>Instead, off to San Diego they went after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/27/cubs-alex-bregman-face-home-runs-red-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-series-padres-world-series" target="_blank" >meaningless 6-2 win Sunday</a> against the Red Sox in St. Petersburg, Florida — look, don’t ask — a 2,000-plus-mile flight during which a travel-weary Cubs team was left to wrestle with some uncomfortable questions.</p><p>“Can we hit anymore?”</p><p>“If we have an ace, where might he be hiding?”</p><p>“Bullpen? What bullpen?”</p><p>And then there are the Sox, who are as experienced at playing postseason baseball as the average bob of seals is at filming TikTok dances. They’ll be in Houston, also starting Tuesday, against a .500 Astros team that owns the distinction of being the worst division champ, by record, in major league history. Despite that, the Sox are the betting underdogs, presumably having something to do with the fact they lost approximately 8.4 billion games from 2023 to 2025.</p><p>Unlike the 89-win Cubs, though, this year’s 84-win Sox finished strong, winning back-to-back-to-back series against the Tigers, Royals and Rockies. Alas, it wasn’t enough to out-sprint the Guardians to the finish line for a division title simply because the Guardians woke up one mid-September morning having inhabited the bodies of the 1927 Yankees. Maybe this is Cleveland’s year to end the majors’ longest current World Series championship drought? It would be a shocker, but it’s possible.</p><p>The Sox, on the other hand? Bless their hearts, they’re just babies.</p><p>Still, you might as well take everything you’ve read thus far in this column, wad it up and drop-kick it onto the nearest trash pile, because this is no time for negativity. It’s only the fourth time both Chicago teams have made it to the postseason, which makes this a mighty big occasion. And can’t we all agree our city was home to baseball’s best two stories this season — the out-of-nowhere emergence of the Sox and the all-out explosion of Cubs MVP-to-be Pete Crow-Armstrong?</p><p>What a thing these Sox have pulled off. Back on Opening Day in Milwaukee, I watched them lose 14-2 to the Brewers and thought: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/26/white-sox-win-total-2026-mlb-opening-day-chris-getz-will-venable-brewers" target="_blank" >Here we go again</a>. But even though general manager Chris Getz and manager Will Venable wouldn’t talk then about what improvement would look like in terms of a number of victories, some around the team were openly confident. TV analyst Steve Stone, a self-described psychic, told me the Sox were going to win “well above” outside expectations. Radio analyst Darrin Jackson thought 80 wins was possible. And second baseman Chase Meidroth had the temerity to use the P-word — “playoffs” — freely.</p><p>“We’re going to compete our asses off,” Meidroth said then.</p><p>I didn’t buy any of it.</p><p>Yeah, well, go suck an egg, Greenberg.</p><p>Despite Getz going in on starting pitcher Luis Castillo at the trade deadline — a failed move — the Sox’ season has been a success no matter what happens against the Astros or, if the Sox actually survive that series, against the Guardians after that.</p><p>Not so for the Cubs, who won’t have anything compelling to hang their hats on if they don’t advance further in Craig Counsell’s third year as manager and Jed Hoyer’s sixth year as president of baseball operations than they did in 2025.</p><p>Last season’s Cubs were good enough to beat the Padres in the wild-card round at Wrigley, but they couldn’t measure up to their prime tormentors, the Brewers, in the divisional round after that. This year, the richest team in the division finished so far behind the small-market Brewers — 14 games — it might take all the gumption the Cubs have just to show their faces in Milwaukee should they get past the Padres again.</p><p>The Cubs were 10-13 in September, but they’ve been less than impressive for a lot longer than that. Over the last four and a half months, they’ve been essentially a .500 team.</p><p>It won’t be as painful in San Diego as the last time the Cubs played playoff baseball there — yep, 1984 — but I don’t think they’ll make it to Milwaukee. An underwhelming season is nearing the end.</p><p>I’ve got the Astros in three, too.</p><p>Either that or a Red Line World Series, right?</p><p>Here we go.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/27/chicago-cubs-white-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-padres-astros-nbc-nbcsn-peacock-streaming-prime-video-xfinity-fubo-youtubetv" >Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/09/24/what-do-i-need-to-know-chicago-cubs-white-sox-both-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >What do I need to know about the Chicago Cubs and White Sox both being in the MLB playoffs?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: White Sox wrap up magical season with victory and still hope to turn page in postseason
entries.summary: <p>In many respects, the 162nd game of the 2026 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> season played out like those of recent years.</p><p>Their 4-2 victory against the Rockies had zero stakes for either side, many reserves filled out the box score and the announced home attendance for the season clocked in at less than 2 million fans (1,986,419).</p><p>The difference was that the nearly 30,000 fans on hand Sunday pushed the full-season figure to the Sox’ highest total since 2022, the only season in the last 15 they’ve eclipsed 2 million fans. Rather than sticking around just in case some lesser-known members of the roster might toss free T-shirts into the stands, fans remained to roar in support of a Sox team headed to Houston for the franchise’s first postseason action in five years.</p><p>It’s easy to imagine a darker context in which an injured pitcher carries one of the highest Q scores on the roster. But the cheers that crested as Mike Vasil raised a fist to the crowd — his other arm around third baseman Miguel Vargas, the Sox’ best player — offered a warm feeling about what this team has become.</p><p>‘‘The way the fans have come out and supported these guys and given them energy, to watch that back-and-forth grow throughout the season has been amazing,’’ manager Will Venable said.</p><p>The Sox won only 84 games, but they did so in front of fans that reasoned 75 victories was an aspirational goal and repaid the unexpected success in enthusiasm.</p><p>Could the Sox have won more? They certainly thought so and rued a slide in early September that cost them the American League Central title.</p><p>They also had 11 walk-off victories and often strung together pitching plans that would have made MacGyver nervous. Plus, no team that has tied itself spiritually to the papacy the way these Sox have can consider themselves starved of blessings.</p><p>‘‘I don’t think anyone saw the kind of success that we had, and I think it was really fun to be a part of,’’ said left-hander Anthony Kay, who earned the victory Sunday.</p><p>The Sox also are boarding their flight to Houston hoping for a reset. They went 34-33 after the All-Star break, allowing the Guardians to catch and overtake them for the division title and dealing them a sting they still were shaking off Sunday.</p><p>‘‘We were pissed,’’ shortstop Colson Montgomery said. ‘‘We had a lot of vocal people. Everyone was just like, ‘We’ve got important games coming up.’ ’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/M409Kh4iA7Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="The White Sox' Colson Montgomery on moving on from the division race and focusing on the playoffs"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Perhaps no one better represents the Sox’ quest for an October rebirth than Montgomery. He socked 31 home runs and was dominant during the 18-10 May that launched the Sox onto the national scene, but he is craving a clean slate after a poor second half. He also set MLB’s single-season strikeout record, about which he admitted, ‘‘You don’t want your name to be a part of.’’</p><p>The Sox dropped five of seven games this season to the Astros across two series that featured some of their lowest moments, strategic moves that Venable openly second-guessed.</p><p>‘‘We were scuffling as a whole,’’ veteran outfielder/designated hitter Randal Grichuk said, referring to the Sox losing three of four games to the Astros in Houston from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. ‘‘We match up well with them.’’</p><p>Are the Sox capable of a deep playoff run? The uncertainty of their rotation suggests otherwise, but that would assume anyone not aboard their flight to Houston understands how and why they have been good all season.</p><p>‘‘Our focus is just on us,’’ designated hitter Andrew Benintendi said. ‘‘Everybody in here knows what we can do.’’</p><p>Would knocking off an 81-81 Astros team be a monumental accomplishment? No. But it’s doable.</p><p>It would be the Sox’ first victory in a postseason series in 21 years. And it would be fun, which is the quality that brought nearly 2 million fans to Rate Field this season.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Alex Bregman homers twice in season-finale win, Cubs head to playoffs aiming to ‘make some noise in October’
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A week after a fouled-off baseball did <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" >significant damage to Alex Bregman’s face</a>, Bregman returned the favor, doling out punishment to the baseballs.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ third baseman launched a pair of home runs as part of a four-hit day in a 6-2 win over the Red Sox in the regular-season finale Sunday, showing the type of impact he can make as the team eyes a deep playoff run.</p><p>“I did want to feel good before the playoffs,” Bregman said. “I wanted my swing to feel like it did right before I got hit. I felt good mechanically today.”</p><p>Bregman, the $175 million free-agent signee who figures to be a key factor in how far this team can go in the postseason, continues to marvel his fellow Cubs with what he’s doing, by merely taking the field so quickly after what happened.</p><p>“I’m not surprised that he’s performing when he’s back on the field. I’m surprised that he’s back on the field,” manager Craig Counsell said. “Him being back on the field is what we should all appreciate and admire.</p><p>“This is not normal that a player is back on the field right now after what he’s been through. You still see what he looks like, frankly, and that tells you what he’s still going through. That’s what I’m surprised by.</p><p>“But his performance, I don’t think it surprises you.”</p><p>Indeed, this is the sort of thing the Cubs long expected from the uber-accomplished Bregman, even back when he was mired in such a deep slump that he was getting booed at Wrigley Field.</p><p>His manager and teammates assumed he would finish the season with the sort of numbers he’s put up throughout his career, and wouldn’t you know it, that’s what happened.</p><p>Thanks to a huge second half, Bregman wrapped the campaign with 28 home runs — the third-highest total of his career — and a right-where-it’s-supposed-to-be .819 OPS.</p><p>“The first four months of the season, I don’t know what that was. I’m embarrassed to have put that on tape,” Bregman said. “But the last two months of the season, that’s who I am as a player. I’m proud to know that, no matter how big of a hole I dug myself, I found my way back out of it and [finished with an OPS] over .800.</p><p>“I learned a lot this year, and I feel like I got better as a pro.”</p><p>After the Cubs scored just nine runs over their five previous games, they wrapped their regular season with a half dozen on Sunday, finally escaping the chilly, windy conditions of Wrigley Field and Fenway Park in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-game-moved-boston-weather-fenway-park-tampa-bay-florida-tropicana-field" >a game relocated to Florida</a>.</p><p>While it might not wipe away all fan concerns over what’s possible in the postseason, it was a good day for the bats — they banged out 13 hits — ahead of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/26/cubs-playoff-matchup-padres-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-postseason-san-diego-phillies-diamondbacks" >a trip to San Diego</a> for a best-of-three playoff series against the Padres.</p><p>There are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/26/cubs-regular-season-finale-playoffs-mlb-postseason-nl-wild-card-standings-offense-lineup-pitching-rotation" >a lot of questions following the Cubs</a> as they head to the West Coast and the lights get their brightest. But their long-held championship-level goals are still in front of them.</p><p>And the belief hasn’t left the clubhouse.</p><p>“When you show up to spring training, that’s what you work the whole offseason for, to start this and be able to play meaningful games in October. That’s exactly what we’ve done,” lefty reliever Ryan Rolison said. “It hasn’t been perfect this year. We’ve been through a lot of adversity, guys stepping up in spots. Now we’re here, and we’re going to make some noise here in October.”</p><p>“When we put games together,” righty reliever Ryan Zeferjahn said, “I don’t know who can beat us.”</p><p>For Bregman, the two-time World Series champ who’s done <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/14/cubs-alex-bregman-career-playoff-games-postseason-world-series-braves-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoff-matchups-carson-kelly-sprint-speed" >more than almost any other hitter in postseason history</a>, he sees in these Cubs the right ingredients for the sort of success he’s had previously in his career.</p><p>“A togetherness. An attention to detail,” he said. “Guys that know what they do well and know what they need to do to prepare.</p><p>“When it comes to the playoffs, it comes down to executing. You’re playing against the best teams in the world. If you do that, you’re in a good spot.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/27/chicago-cubs-white-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-padres-astros-nbc-nbcsn-peacock-streaming-prime-video-xfinity-fubo-youtubetv" >Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV
entries.summary: <p>Chicago baseball fans got the shaft when MLB released the schedule Sunday for the Cubs’ and White Sox’ wild-card series. NBC has the rights to the first-round matchups, but Games 1 and 2 for the Cubs and Sox were relegated to the network’s streaming service, Peacock, and NBC Sports Network, to which you might not have access.</p><p>The ballyhooed Red Sox-Yankees rivalry — which the nation always is subjected to more than necessary — naturally was given the prime-time spot on over-the-air NBC for the first two games of its series. The network also will air the first two games of the Phillies-Braves series in the afternoon. The best-of-three wild-card series are scheduled to run Tuesday to Thursday.</p><p>To watch Games 1 and 2 of Cubs-Padres and White Sox-Astros, fans must watch on Peacock, which costs $12.99 per month, or NBCSN, which is available on Comcast’s Xfinity system and streamers Fubo and YouTube TV. Though Xfinity and YouTube TV are two of the largest pay-TV providers in the country, NBCSN is missing from services such as DirecTV and Astound/RCN.</p><p>For the Sox, Games 1 and 2 are scheduled for 4 p.m. For the Cubs, they’re set for 9. The start time for a possible Game 3 of either series will depend on how many series are still going.</p><p>These aren’t the first major postseason games stuck on a streamer. The NFL put the Packers-Bears playoff game in January on Prime Video, but it was available locally over the air. The NBA streamed 28 first- and second-round playoff games exclusively on Peacock (seven, which also aired on NBCSN) and Prime Video (21) last season.</p><p>But they are the first MLB postseason games to air on a streaming service. It was part of NBC’s deal that gave it “Sunday Night Baseball,” which had aired on ESPN for 36 seasons, and the wild-card round. The rest of the American League playoffs will air on TBS; Fox and FS1 have the rest of the National League playoffs. The World Series will air on Fox.</p><p>Here’s some good news: NBC will continue its use of local analysts on national broadcasts. Steve Stone will be on the call for the Sox’ series, and Jim Deshaies will be in the booth for the Cubs’ series.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest
